speechtext:
I do not want to speak for any length of time, but I think I should say a few words on the question whether or not ithe United Farmers of Alberta were opposed to the five cent bonus on wheat. Before I come to that, however, I wish to refer to the terms of the resolution, and the proposal that the bonus be paid on an acreage basis. On the whole I believe it would be fairer if something of that kind could be worked out, but I would add this proviso, that only land in fit shape for putting in a crop should be considered, and that would be one of the difficulties in administering a plan of that kind.
I do not think I need argue that the five cent bonus on wheat was generally acceptable to the farmers of western Canada, because I hiave not heard of one farmer who turned it down. I think that should be answer enough to anyone who considers that the five cent bonus was not acceptable on grounds of principle or on any other grounds whatsoever. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) read the resolution that was passed at 'the convention of the United Farmers of ALberta. That resolution reads:
Therefore be it resolved, that we ask the Dominion government, through our board of directors, to change the bonus payment to the effect that all grain growers be recompensed to a minimum of at least one dollar an acre seeded, so that all those who have received no bonus and all those who would not otherwise receive this amount should be treated fairly, and to those whose crop production exceeds this amount the bonus to be as it is at the present time. . . .
A resolution was introduced at the convention after that. It came from my own constituency, but I do not think I am to blame for its having come to the convention. However, it came from Grande Prairie, and here it is:
Whereas we appreciate the bonus on wheat by the Dominion government being a step in the right direction; and whereas there is no bonus on other agricultural products:
Therefore be it resolved that we demand that the Dominion government bonus agricultural production and that the amount of bonus be in proportion to the benefits enjoyed by the manufacturers through the tariff.
Some of the delegates at the convention of the United Farmers of Alberta thought that we were going just a little too far in asking for that, and they voted it down, and some of the people who were behind this resolution thought that they were treated unfairly and requested a reconsideration of the first one passed, but they could not get that one reconsidered or rescinded. That explains the newspaper stories that have come to eastern Canada to the effect that the convention was opposed to the bonus on wheat.
I should like to point out to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) that the average price received for wheat by the farmers in western Canada is around 38 or 40 cents. A lot of them sold their wheat for 30 cents a bushel last fall.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: At the elevator?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
At the
elevator. Wheat went up to 50 cents or a little better, but a good many of them did not have sense enough to sell at that price. Possibly somewhere between 35 and 40 cents is the average price received for No. 1 northern but it is not all No. 1. Now that is not the cost of producing wheat; you cannot produce wheat for that. If, therefore, as I believe, the general economic conditions in Canada are largely determined by the volume of wheat purchasing power of the western farmers, it is necessary to continue, until the price of wheat rises, to bonus wheat considerably, and I hope that the government will seriously consider carrying on even though it may have considerable difficulty in doing so.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate had it not been for the statement by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) that the only people in Canada who were asked to give notes in return for relief were the farmers of the west. That statement was corrected by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks), but I find it repeated with even greater
Farm Reliej-Mr. Turnbull

emphasis by the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in his address. The fact is that the citizens of my city are being asked to repay any moneys they get during this winter by way of relief.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
It is not a shame, because the people of my own city are asking for it. They are not asking for charity. They are asking authorities to assist them temporarily over a period of strain, and those gentlemen who say shame do not know the people of the city of Regina, because those people wish to stand on their own feet. They who say shame represent those who are not ashamed to take money that is not coming to them.
As regards the giving of notes in Saskatchewan, I am strongly of the impression that those notes are not given as a result of pressure brought to bear upon the people either by the federal or by the provincial authorities. There are hundreds and thousands of men in Saskatchewan who have said that they would not take any money by way of relief but would starve first unless they got the opportunity of repaying the money advanced them. There are citizens of that type all through Saskatchewan and I am sorry that my hon. friends opposite, apparently, have not met more of them.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: May I ask whether the manufacturers helped out in this crisis are promising to give back afterwards the favours given them?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I am not concerned at all with any of your friends the manufacturers. I am particularly concerned with my own people in Saskatchewan and I say that notes have been given by the farmers of that province largely because those farmers are used to standing as far as possible on their own feet and want to continue to do so. For that reason representations were made by many farmers to members of this house and of the government that they be allowed to repay the moneys advanced to them. There has appeared in the public press of the country within the last week, from those in charge.of relief work in Saskatchewan, a report that already some of those who have received assistance in that province are making arrangements for the return of the money they have been given and are asking for statements of account so that they may begin their repayment. I know there are some who do not wish to sign notes.
I had the privilege of addressing a meeting in the constituency of the hon. member for Mel-

ville (Mr, Motherwell) last fall, and at the close of the meeting one of the hon. gentleman's constituents came to me and asked whether the government was going to request the repayment of the money. I said I thought the Saskatchewan Relief Commission would, and he said, "If they are going to, I don't want it." I said, "Well, my friend, if that is the way you feel about it I shall be glad to see that you don't get it."

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Were you in a position to prevent him from getting relief?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I used what influence I had to see that he did not get it without signing a note for it, and I did so on representations from a great many respectable citizens of Saskatchewan who did not wish to take relief without signing notes. The relief commission in Saskatchewan which is administering relief in the southern part of the province, in whose favour the notes are drawn, and whose recommendations are largely followed in the policy laid down in that province, is a non-political body including representatives of the farmers and of the Labour party. It is quite true that the majority are Conservatives, but it is equally true that those who represent the Liberal party and the farmers' party in that province are not, so far as the administration of relief is concerned, at variance with other members of the commission.
I think that possibly one of the troubles about the resolution brought before the house is the fact that the resolution itself recognizes the absolute impossibility of providing for all classes of people on an equitable basis, because neither the resolution itself nor those supporting it suggest any solution that would be absolutely equitable. It is quite true that the hon. member for Weyburn and the hon. member for Melville suggest that the men who have given promissory notes be given credit at some time or other for a certain amount of money on those notes. That does not apply to many people who did not ask for relief, to those who went out on their own scheme rather than apply to the government for relief. It is impossible to have an absolutely equitable system. If the representations of the Saskatchewan Rural Municipalities Association had been made in May or June of 1931 they might have been considered more favourably but, as I understand it, those resolutions were formally presented to the government in December, 1931, when the relief commission had been launched and when it was impossible to make the necessary changes.

Farm Relief-Mr. Turnbull
The situation which has arisen to-day apparently arises from a confusion of ideas. The five cent bonus was applied for a certain purpose, and hon. members are complaining because it did not happen to fit another purpose. This bonus was to be a cure for a certain condition and because it did not cure a totally different condition, hon. members are complaining. The five cent bonus was granted to meet the complaint made by the farmers of western Canada and by hon. members opposite, among others, that agriculture in western Canada was losing money on every bushel of wheat produced. It was contended that the farmer was not able to raise wheat, not only at a profit but at a price to cover the cost of production. It was to meet that condition that the bonus of five cents was granted. It was a bonus on the production of wheat, not a bonus to those who did not produce, no matter whose fault it may have been.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Was not that measure in a sense a relief measure?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: In my judgment it was not- a relief measure, it was a bonus to industry. It was no more a relief measure than was the bonus given a few years ago to the steel industry. That bonus was granted to enable them to produce steel at a price to compete in the markets of the world.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Is not a bonus
given under those circumstances a form of relief?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Not the form of relief
we are talking about. That is my judgment but the hon. member may have his own conviction. The bonus was granted to enable farmers to produce wheat at a price which would enable them to sell it in the markets of the world.
Another condition arose; a large number of farmers had no wheat, either because of crop failure or from the effects of hail or something of that kind.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Does the
hon. member realize that the act was passed on August 3?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: I realize that.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
The hon
member said the condition arose later.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Did I say "later"?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
I do not think I did.
As my hon. friend well knows, the budget which contained this provision was brought 41761-20
down on June 1. As I see it, that provision was not intended to apply to crop failures, whether or not it was known at that time such crop failures did exist; it was intended as a bonus on the production of wheat.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: At that time it was an export bonus.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: The interruption of my hon. friend has nothing whatever to do with the argument.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Oh, yfes, it has.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Not a thing. Another
condition arose in western Canada, a complete crop failure, in some districts extending back for two years and in others for three years. When this bonus was introduced the government said that this condition would have to be taken care of by other means, and it has been taken care of fairly well. The Saskatchewan Relief Commission has provided the things necessary to maintain these people and their cattle through the present winter. I do not know of one person in Saskatchewan who has starved, everyone who needed it has been supplied with fuel, food, clothing and shelter.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Do I understand that those who produced the wheat received a five cent bonus while those who unfortunately had none will be obliged to pay for the relief granted by way of bonus?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Those who produced
wheat received the bonus.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Those who did not, pay for the relief.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Those who did not produce wheat did not receive the bonus.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
But they paid for the
relief-

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Not yet.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: -by way of the bonus.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
At the request of a
great many people in Saskatchewan, those who received relief were given the privilege of repayment. This had a deterrent effect upon some people-

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: The people who were worse off actually paid by means of the notes.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
-I am happy to say the number is few-who had the intention to hold out both hands for relief when, in fact, they did not need it. Other measures were taken to provide for those who did not have a crop. There were measures taken to supply

Farm Relief-Mr. Gershaw

them with the necessities to carry on through the winter, and other measures were adopted to supply seed and feed for the spring and to grant the necessary assistance to put the crop in the ground. The suggestion has been made that those who buy this seed and feed will have to pay the five cent bonus. Wheat was quoted yesterday on the Winnipeg exchange at 66 cents per bushel, but I venture to say the farmer in Saskatchewan will receive his feed and seed for considerably less than 66 cents per bushel.
Two conditions existed; the bonus was applied to one and the relief was applied to the other. The policy of taking back notes may be right or wrong but I do not intend to argue that matter. All I am trying to point out is that it is not right to apply to one disease the cure for another. It may be said that the second cure was not the proper one, but I am not concerned with that; it can be argued at another time. It is owing to this confusion that the present resolution has been introduced.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the constituency which I have the honour to represent adjoins the constituency of Acadia, and the description of the difficulties faced by the farmers in that constituency as given by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) applies to the farmers in my constituency. During the last few months I attended a large number of gatherings of farmers, and at each a resolution was passed, usually unanimously, in favour of having the bonus paid in some other way or upon some other basis, the acreage basis being the one usually chosen. The fanners realized the difficulties in checking up, but felt that under present conditions the amount of money paid was not applied in such a way as to give the most relief.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN FEDERAL ASSISTANCE ON BUSHEL RATHER THAN ACREAGE BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a notice of motion which stood in my name asked for the production of certain communications which had passed between the government and different organizations in the province of Saskatchewan. I mentioned this matteT this afternoon to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and he said he would telephone immediately and endeavour to get these communications to me. Just this minute I am in receipt of one of the documents asked for, but I would like to have all the documents asked for in my motion, so that when this debate is resumed I will be able to deal more intelligently with this matter. At this time, I would like to have it called six o'clock. The Prime Minister very kindly told me he would get them and

that if he was not able to get them, he would have the debate adjourned so that I might have an opportunity of discussing the matter. There are also some others who wish to speak.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, February 18, 1932
